from:
## The Space Between 0 and 1

Count out loud: 1, 2, 3, 4. Easy. Now count what is *between* 1 and 2.

There is a whole world in there, and fractions are how we name the places inside it.

Start with a number line. Put 0 at the left and 1 at the right. That whole trip from 0 to 1 is the **whole**, and every fraction in this lesson is a piece of it. Cut it into two equal pieces and you get **halves**. Now cut the same space into **4 equal pieces** instead. The cuts land on new places, and each place has a name: one-fourth, two-fourths, three-fourths. Written as numbers: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4. One single piece of that size is called a **unit** fraction, so 1/4 is one unit of a fourth.

The bottom number — the **denominator** — tells you *how many equal pieces the whole was cut into*. The top number — the **numerator** — tells you *how many of those pieces you counted from zero*.

So 3/4 is not a pizza. It is a **location**. Walk three of the four steps from 0 toward 1 and stop. That is where 3/4 lives.

Here is where the number line earns its keep. Look at 2/4. Now look at 1/2. They land on the exact same spot. Same location, two names. That is what **equivalent fractions** means — different words, same place, like a friend who goes by a nickname.

The number line also fixes the most common fraction mistake. When you **compare** two fractions, you are really asking which one sits farther from 0. Which is bigger, 1/4 or 1/8? Many people say 1/8, because 8 is bigger than 4. But look: cutting the space into 8 pieces makes each piece *smaller*. So 1/8 sits closer to 0, and 1/4 is bigger. **More pieces means smaller pieces.** The number line shows you that instantly, and it never lies.

One more thing. Fractions do not stop at 1. Keep going: 5/4 is one step past 1. Fractions are just numbers, and the number line goes on forever in both directions. Once you see fractions as places instead of slices, they stop being a special weird topic and become ordinary numbers — which is exactly what they are.

## The Space Between 0 and 1

Count out loud: 1, 2, 3, 4. Easy. Now count what is *between* 1 and 2.

There is a whole world in there, and fractions are how we name the places inside it.

Start with a number line. Put 0 at the left and 1 at the right. That whole trip from 0 to 1 is the **whole**, and this distance sets the size of one whole. Fractions greater than 1 extend beyond it. Cut it into two equal pieces and you get **halves**. Now cut the same space into **4 equal pieces** instead. The cuts land on new places, and each place has a name: one-fourth, two-fourths, three-fourths. Written as numbers: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4. One single piece of that size is called a **unit** fraction, so 1/4 is one unit of a fourth.

The bottom number — the **denominator** — tells you *how many equal pieces the whole was cut into*. The top number — the **numerator** — tells you *how many of those pieces you counted from zero*.

A picture of equal pizza slices can model 3/4, and 3/4 is also a number with a **location**. Walk three of the four steps from 0 toward 1 and stop. That is where 3/4 lives.

Here is where the number line earns its keep. Look at 2/4. Now look at 1/2. They land on the exact same spot. Same location, two names. That is what **equivalent fractions** means — different words, same place, like a friend who goes by a nickname.

The number line also fixes the most common fraction mistake. When you **compare** two fractions, you are really asking which one sits farther to the right. For these positive fractions, that also means farther from 0. Which is bigger, 1/4 or 1/8? Many people say 1/8, because 8 is bigger than 4. But look: cutting the space into 8 pieces makes each piece *smaller*. So 1/8 sits closer to 0, and 1/4 is bigger. **For the same whole, more equal pieces means smaller unit fractions.** The number line shows you that instantly, and it never lies.

One more thing. Fractions do not stop at 1. Keep going: 5/4 is one step past 1. Fractions are just numbers, and the number line goes on forever in both directions. Once you see fractions as places instead of slices, they stop being a special weird topic and become ordinary numbers — which is exactly what they are.

from.target: Equivalent fractions: same spot, two names
essentialFacts: 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same spot on the number line.
Equivalent fractions are different names for the same place.
4/8 and 3/6 are also names for that halfway spot.
from.aiExample: Picture one friend standing exactly halfway down a hallway. Her name tag says 1/2 on one side and 2/4 on the other. Two tags, one person, one spot.
from.mapping: The friend is the location. The tags are the names. The single spot in the hallway is the number line. So equivalent means two tags on one person, not two people.
from.scaffoldStarter: One person stands at ____. Her tags say ____ and ____.
scaffoldSteps: Draw or picture a hallway from 0 to 1.
Put one person at the halfway spot with two name tags.
Add a third tag that also belongs there.
coachPrompts: Could 3/4 be a tag on the same person? Why not?
from.studentPrompt: Make your own one-spot, two-names picture.
from.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture show what equivalent means?

from: Sharing one candy bar with 4 friends versus 8 friends — bigger group, smaller share.
to: Share one candy bar equally among 4 people, or an identical bar equally among 8 people. Each person in the group of 4 gets the larger share.

from: The reading says 3/4 is a location, not a pizza slice. What does that mean?
to: What does it mean to describe 3/4 as a location on the number line?

from: When the denominator gets bigger, each piece gets ____, because ____.
to: For the same whole, when the denominator gets bigger, each unit fraction gets ____, because ____.

from: Because almost nothing in real life comes in whole numbers. Half an hour, three-quarters of a cup, a quarter mile. Whole numbers alone cannot measure the world.
to: Fractions help us name parts of an amount, such as half an hour or three-fourths of a cup. Whole numbers alone cannot name every amount.

from: Yes! Same location on the number line, two ways of writing it. Decimals are just fractions where the denominator is always 10, 100, 1000, and so on.
to: Yes. Both land at the same point: 0.5 = 5/10 = 1/2. Some fractions have decimals that keep repeating. For example, 1/3 = 0.333... .

from: Absolutely. 5/4 just means you walked five fourth-sized steps, which takes you past 1. Those are called improper fractions, though there is nothing improper about them.
to: Yes. 5/4 means five steps of size one-fourth from zero. You pass 1 and reach 1 1/4. It is called an improper fraction.

from: Because 8 is bigger than 4, and your brain is pattern-matching to whole numbers. It is the single most common fraction mistake — which is why the number line is worth drawing every time.
to: You may be thinking that 8 is larger than 4. But with the same whole, cutting it into eight equal pieces makes each piece smaller than one of four equal pieces. Draw both on the same line.

from: What is the biggest fraction between 0 and 1?
to: What is the biggest fraction strictly between 0 and 1?

from: There is no biggest one, and that is the wild part. You can always get closer to 1: 99/100, then 999/1000, forever. Between any two fractions there is always another.
to: There is no biggest one. Pick a fraction below 1. The point halfway from it to 1 is a larger fraction that is still below 1. You can do this again.

from: They do — negative one-half sits exactly as far left of 0 as one-half sits right of it. You will work with those more in later grades.
to: Yes. Negative one-half is as far left of zero as one-half is to the right.

from: More pieces means smaller pieces: 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/4.
to: For the same whole, more equal pieces means smaller unit fractions: 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/4.
